The global building boom of power-hungry data centers is straining electrical grids. But by applying AI to rethink how large cloud-computing systems operate, Christina Delimitrou seeks to make data centers more energy-efficient.

Oct 8, 2026 Full story Share: 
Twitter

Research and Education that Matter
MIT for America

Addressing a national need, the MIT for America initiative ranges across STEM fields and will engage students from kindergarten through community college, preparing them to live and work in a world increasingly shaped by science and technology. 

Treating tremors

The startup Encora Therapeutics began as a project in 2.009, MIT’s iconic product-design class, to help people with Parkinson's disease. Now, nine years later, the FDA has cleared Encora’s device to help adults with essential tremor. 

 

Healthier aging

Researchers developed a noninvasive way to identify senescent cells — which are still alive but have stopped dividing — within aging tissue. The advance could help diagnose age-related disorders and guide scientists working on new treatments.

From MIT to the Marines

Always up for a challenge, Braedon Rudolph ’26 double majored in physics and economics before commissioning as an officer in the Marines. He also played lacrosse, composed music, and consulted for nuclear energy organizations.

Supporting our Jewish community

This fact sheet offers a high-level summary of the many steps MIT leaders have taken to support our vibrant Jewish community.

Benefits for all Americans

MIT’s vital research and education — on topics such as human health, energy innovation, quantum computing, and advanced manufacturing — continue to advance national security, economic competitiveness, and quality of life for all Americans.

1∕3 Next
 
August 27 – December 4
Practicing Pluralism
In 2026, as we mark Deborah Berke’s tenth year as dean, the Yale School of Architecture mounts an exhibition that examines the trajectory of its pedagogy under her leadership. As the world experiences even greater strains on our population growth, urban infrastructure, and climate, architecture at Yale has increasingly been explored as a practice of social engagement. Dean Berke’s focus on this imperative has led her to attract and recruit advanced studio faculty who see architecture as a means through which to inquire about and intervene in cultural-spatial questions. This exhibition features one project each from twenty-one architects who have taught advanced studios at Yale between 2016 and 2026. Despite the plurality of their design approaches, the architects represented are united around the core assertion that architecture holds the ability to address some of the world’s most pressing questions. The exhibition grounds itself in YSoA’s time-honored tradition of pluralism, here marking its evolution from an openness to stylistic diversity to the structural incorporation of numerous worldviews and design methodologies. Through a variety of media, the projects in this exhibition illustrate recent, current, and future-forward methods and design attitudes that shape Yale School of Architecture’s distinct culture. In this exhibition and at YSoA, pluralism is an ongoing, ever-evolving practice.
 
October 8 – November 7
Common Reed
Common Reed explores the cultural ecology of the common reed (Phragmites australis) through parallel studies of its reciprocal relationships with landscapes and built environments in Iraq, England, and China. The exhibition brings tangible and tactile encounters into the North Gallery through workshops and installations that explore the potential of Phragmites in architectural practice.
 
January 14, 2027 – July 3, 2027
Sir John Soane: The Poetry of Architecture
This exhibition brings together an exceptional selection of architectural drawings, rare architectural treatises, models and contemporary parallels to explore the life, work, and enduring influence of the British neoclassical architect Sir John Soane (1753–1837). Organized around themes including collecting, architectural practice, education and legacy, it reveals how Soane redefined the language of classicism through originality, technical innovation, and a profound sensitivity to purpose and place. Drawn primarily from the collections of Sir John Soane’s Museum, historical works are presented alongside twentieth- and twenty-first-century architecture inspired in some way by Soane–such as Rudolph Hall at Yale–creating a dialogue across time. Together, they demonstrate that classicism is not a fixed historical style but a living tradition, highlighting the continuing relevance of Soane’s vision and its lasting capacity to inspire architecture today.
